A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same 667-puzzle PuzzleWorld benchmark. Their text, tables, figures, and appendices are readable and support comparison, including matching material moved between sections and renumbered appendices.

before.justification: v1 reports original model evaluations, controlled fine-tuning results, judge validation, contamination testing, and error analyses.

after.justification: v2 retains those experiments and adds model evaluations, measured novice and enthusiast performance, downstream transfer results, and robustness analyses. The expert scores are explicitly assumed rather than directly measured.

M1.justification: The benchmark construction, annotation schema, prompting, and stepwise grading procedure remain substantively unchanged. Appendix D.3 explains alternative-path credit already supported by v1's grading prompt. Added model configurations and transfer experiments do not introduce a new proposed architecture, objective, or inference algorithm.

E1.justification: v1's experiments focus on PuzzleWorld. v2 adds actual transfer evaluation on Rebus puzzles and MathVista tasks covering geometry, textbook questions, math word problems, and visual question answering. It also adds human puzzle-solving evaluation across novice and enthusiast populations. The original 667-puzzle corpus remains unchanged.

E2.justification: Table 2 adds Claude Opus 4, Gemini 2.5 Pro, Gemini 3 Pro, and Grok 4, alongside measured human novice and enthusiast comparisons. An assumed expert ceiling is also displayed. The original five evaluated models and the answer-only fine-tuning control are retained.

E3.justification: New protocols include nine participants per human group solving four puzzles each with one hour per puzzle, paired transcription conditions, and separate 10% paraphrasing studies. The original 80/20 fine-tuning split and InternVL3 LoRA settings remain. Transfer settings are inconsistent: Section 5.3 and Table 4 identify InternVL3, whereas Appendix F.2 specifies full-parameter Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct training.

E4.justification: v2 adds an OCR comparison on a 5% text-only subset, a visual-forgetting case study, separate robustness tests paraphrasing candidate solutions and reference annotations, and difficulty-by-modality analyses in Tables 5–6. The original contamination test and myopic-reasoning, language-bottleneck, and sketching analyses are retained rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: Appendix D.2 introduces a paired t-test for performance with versus without transcription, reporting t = 0.52 and p > 0.1. The new paraphrasing studies reuse the correlation, significance, and MAE reporting approach already present in v1's judge validation. Neither version reports repeated-seed uncertainty or confidence intervals for the main model scores.

E6.justification: The original Table 2 model scores and Table 3 fine-tuning results are retained. New results include Gemini 3 Pro at 18.00% answer accuracy and 39.99% stepwise accuracy, plus human novice and enthusiast answer accuracies of 13.89% and 44.44%. Table 4 adds mixed transfer results: Rebus improves from 3.2% to 5.1% and visual QA from 32.40% to 39.11%, while textbook QA falls from 63.92% to 60.13% and math word problems from 62.37% to 59.14%. Additional robustness and difficulty results are also reported.

T1.justification: The reasoning-step tuple and latest-successful-reference-step scoring definition are retained. Expanded discussion of creative solutions and grading behavior adds explanations, without new formal definitions, mathematical derivations, theorems, or proofs.

C1.justification: The benchmark contribution remains, but v2 elevates transfer to downstream visual reasoning into a central claim in the abstract and conclusion. It also introduces claims comparing models with human novices and enthusiasts. The abstract updates the best answer accuracy from 14% to 18%, although the introduction still retains the earlier 14% statement.

C2.justification: v2 substantially expands interpretation and limitations concerning alternative solution paths, judge hallucinations, shortcut answers, abstract puzzles as proxies for practical reasoning, and barriers to incorporating harder puzzle sources. It adds interpretations of visual forgetting, selective transfer, and human versus model modality sensitivity. The original three principal failure mechanisms remain.

D1.justification: Appendix F.2 adds a transfer-training recipe using Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct, full-parameter updates, learning rate 1e-5, and five epochs. Human evaluation details and the provenance of difficulty labels are also expanded. Existing hardware, InternVL3 LoRA settings, prompts, and annotation instructions are retained. The transfer recipe conflicts with the main text's InternVL3 attribution, limiting reproducibility.

R1.justification: v2 adds positioning against FineReason and lateral-thinking benchmarks, plus references supporting constrained-domain reasoning, transfer, and visual forgetting. It updates frontier-model references and removes the earlier general model-ecosystem discussion. The central positioning around open-ended puzzlehunts and the comparison with EnigmaEval remain intact.

P1.justification: The introduction is substantially rewritten and reordered, explanations throughout are tightened, and the conclusion is recast around diagnosis and transfer. The contamination section moves into Appendix E.1, and the appendix organization is extensively expanded and rearranged. Author ordering, contribution markers, affiliations, and publication headers also change.

P2.justification: Table 2 is expanded and organized into open-model, closed-model, and human groups. v2 adds the transfer table, two difficulty tables, and the visual-forgetting figure. Existing figures and puzzle samples are retained with caption, sizing, and placement changes, while the paper is re-typeset in the ICLR format with running headers and revised table emphasis.

improvement.justification: Compared with v1, the measured human reference and targeted OCR and scoring checks provide better context and empirical support for interpreting the benchmark. However, the transfer model is inconsistently identified between Section 5.3/Table 4 and Appendix F.2, expert performance is assumed, and paraphrasing only narrowly tests alternative reasoning and annotation noise. The additions provide a useful net improvement, but these limitations constrain the strength and reproducibility of the expanded claims.
